threat_statement: An attacker could exhaust, block, or disable EKS Kubernetes API server after availability and resource-protection controls are insufficient, resulting in the damage described by DS_01: The EKS API server is the single control point through which all workload changes on the diagnostic platform cluster are submitted and all cluster reads are served. If its availability is compromised, the cluster stops accepting requests entirely — deployments, scaling and secret rotation all fail, crashed workloads cannot be restarted, and every technician session opened against the web diagnostic platform fails to load.
derivation_note: availability maps to denial_of_service under the STRIDE taxonomy. This deterministic fallback was used because the model did not return the required submit_threat tool call after two attempts.

threat_statement: An attacker could invoke privileged operations through EKS Kubernetes API server after authorization enforcement is bypassed, resulting in the damage described by DS_02: The EKS API server evaluates IAM/OIDC identity together with Kubernetes RBAC rules to decide which identities may read secrets, create workloads and reach other namespaces. If its authorization is compromised, those scope decisions stop holding: an identity that is authenticated at all can read platform secrets and alter or delete workloads beyond its assigned permissions, so the separation between dealership tenants, platform teams and production namespaces is lost.
derivation_note: authorization maps to elevation_of_privilege under the STRIDE taxonomy. This deterministic fallback was used because the model did not return the required submit_threat tool call after two attempts.

threat_statement: An attacker could gain unauthorized access to data or responses exposed by EKS worker nodes after access-control or data-exposure safeguards are bypassed, resulting in the damage described by DS_03: The EKS worker nodes are the single compute substrate for the whole platform: every service pod, in-flight diagnostic payload, customer PII record, and cached service credential runs in memory on these Graviton instances, and each node also serves the instance metadata endpoint that hands out the workload's IAM role credentials. If their confidentiality is compromised, the platform's most sensitive data becomes readable and copyable in one place, including live session tokens, IMDS-issued AWS credentials, and diagnostic records that exist only in process memory and are never written to a log or backup for later review.
derivation_note: confidentiality maps to information_disclosure under the STRIDE taxonomy. This deterministic fallback was used because the model did not return the required submit_threat tool call after two attempts.

threat_statement: EKS worker nodes: An attacker who first gains write access to the EKS cluster — for example by recovering a service-account kubeconfig or an over-permissive IAM role from the pipeline that pushes workloads — next uses it to rewrite the Deployments, DaemonSets, and kubelet/pod configuration of the workloads that validate licenses, process diagnostic results, and compute OTA update state, replacing their container images with locally built unsigned artifacts that the node admits without a signature or provenance check, so the compromised code on the worker node silently returns falsified diagnostic readings, forged license validation outcomes, and manipulated update decisions that the rest of the system accepts as trustworthy.
derivation_note: Derived from DS_04 for AS_02 (EKS worker nodes, integrity). The mechanism unique to this asset is that the worker node is simultaneously the trust anchor and the execution environment: the kubelet pulls whatever image the pod spec names, so anything that can edit a pod spec or the images the node accepts can redefine the results of every workload scheduled there. Attack path — Step 1: Attacker exfiltrates a cluster credential (kubeconfig token, CI service-account, or IAM role assumed by the workload-deploying pipeline) from a leaked config repo, secret, or overly broad role binding. Step 2 (circumvent step): Attacker authenticates with a legitimate-looking identity and calls the Kubernetes API, but the RBAC/namespace scope permits patching Deployments, DaemonSets, and ConfigMaps, and no admission policy (Kyverno/Gatekeeper image signature verification) blocks an unsigned image, so the patch is accepted. Step 3: Attacker points the image reference at a registry artifact they control, or mounts a hostPath/privileged pod to patch node-local binaries and configuration, and the kubelet pulls or accepts the substituted content. Step 4: The license validator, diagnostic result processor, and OTA state machine now execute attacker-controlled code and emit falsified output; because the response payloads are not signed or independently verified downstream, consumers record the fabricated values as legitimate. STRIDE: Tampering (data/code modification at the processing layer, aligned with ISO 21434 clause 15.6). OWASP: A08 Software and Data Integrity Failures — no verification of the integrity/authenticity of the code and data the update/pipeline path delivers.

threat_statement: An attacker could alter data, configuration, or processing performed by Envoy Gateway + public NLB (envoy-gateway-lb) after integrity validation or change controls are bypassed, resulting in the damage described by DS_05: This component is the single front door for the Cloud API, terminating TLS on port 443 and routing each inbound request to the intended in-cluster service. If its integrity is compromised, the last trusted hop in every request path can no longer be assumed to behave as declared: requests may be routed to the wrong service, headers and request bodies may be altered in transit, certificates that do not belong to this platform may be accepted, and responses returned to API clients may not be the ones the addressed service actually produced, so clients act on data that never came from the backend they queried.
derivation_note: integrity maps to tampering under the STRIDE taxonomy. This deterministic fallback was used because the model did not return the required submit_threat tool call after two attempts.

threat_statement: Envoy Gateway + public NLB (envoy-gateway-lb): An attacker who learns the public NLB DNS name for the Envoy Gateway simply sends a large volume of concurrent TCP connections and near-complete TLS ClientHello records so that the load balancer's connection table and Envoy's TLS handshake worker pool saturate, and because no WAF, CloudFront distribution, or second load balancer sits in front to shed the traffic and no connection-rate limit or handshake timeout is configured on the gateway itself, every legitimate external call to the Cloud API now stalls or fails at connection establishment or TLS handshake, simultaneously cutting off the diagnostic, vehicle data, and account endpoints behind it with no redundant path to fail over to.
derivation_note: The damage scenario is purely availability loss of AS_03, the sole ingress path, so the STRIDE category is denial_of_service. The specific action is connection-flood plus slow-TLS-handshake exhaustion against the public NLB and Envoy gateway, not volumetric bandwidth saturation (which would imply a CDN or scrubbing tier exists — it does not). The mechanism is unique to this asset: it is simultaneously the internet-facing load balancer and the TLS-terminating proxy, so resource exhaustion at the handshake stage kills the entire cluster's external API surface. The missing controls cited are the absent WAF/CloudFront/second NLB and the absence of rate limiting and aggressive handshake timeouts on the gateway. Mapped to OWASP A04 Insecure Design (architecture with a single unreplicated ingress and no abuse control) and API4 Unrestricted Resource Consumption, since the attack consumes handshake and connection resources rather than bypassing authentication or corrupting data.

threat_statement: An attacker could invoke privileged operations through Kong API gateway after authorization enforcement is bypassed, resulting in the damage described by DS_07: The Kong API gateway is the single front door for the /core/v2, /data/v2 and /pandora/v1 routes, executing the authentication plugins, rate limits and per-route access rules that decide which caller may reach which backend service and which records it may see. If its authorization is compromised, a caller holding a valid but limited token is served the routes, vehicle records, diagnostic data or subscription entitlements that were never granted to it — responses come back as ordinary successes, so access outside the caller's scope is handed out silently and without any indication that a policy was bypassed.
derivation_note: authorization maps to elevation_of_privilege under the STRIDE taxonomy. This deterministic fallback was used because the model did not return the required submit_threat tool call after two attempts.

threat_statement: Hasura GraphQL engine: An authenticated but low-privilege caller holding a Hasura session-role JWT for a single tenant first gains access to the GraphQL endpoint, then submits a query or mutation whose selection set traverses a nested relationship field — or hits a table, column, or check/remote-join path — that the role's allow-list and row filter do not cover, because Hasura applies row filters and column/field permissions per selection set so the filter applied to the top-level root field does not extend to the rows reached through the related field, and the result is that the caller successfully reads and updates core database records belonging to other tenants and to roles it was never granted, breaking the permission boundary for every application that uses this single GraphQL entry point.
derivation_note: Derived from DS_08 against AS_05 (Hasura GraphQL engine, CIAAAN property: authorization). The damage scenario names the mechanism uniquely to this asset: Hasura's authorization model is enforced per root field per selection set, and row-level filters on the top-level query do not automatically propagate to rows resolved through nested relationship fields. That indirection is what lets a limited session-role JWT cross tenant boundaries, so the threat is classified as elevation of privilege (gaining rights beyond those granted) rather than a generic broken-access-control finding on any API. The primary attack action is navigating an authorized top-level query into a nested field or an uncovered table where the role's permissions are absent, then reading and modifying those rows. Mapped to OWASP A01 Broken Access Control (with A05 relevant if the exposure is a permissive allow-list/role configuration), consistent with the Layer 3 mapping table where A01 maps to Elevation of Privilege. Chosen over information disclosure because the scenario includes unauthorized modification of records, not only unauthorized reading.

threat_statement: Aurora cloudapi database: An attacker first sends a request to the Cloud API front door carrying a crafted tenant or subscription value that the front door concatenates into a SQL statement instead of binding as a parameter, and because the cloudapi database user holds UPDATE and DELETE grants on the tenant_role_bindings and policy_rules tables rather than read-only access, that injected statement upserts a fleet_admin binding for a tenant the attacker controls and drops a restrictive policy row, so from the next request onward the front door returns other tenants' vehicle records and authorizes remote actions the approved role was never scoped for while legitimate calls begin failing, and the modified role and policy tables can no longer serve as evidence of what access was actually permitted.
derivation_note: Derived specifically for AS_06 because this database is not a passive data store — it is the live authorization source the front door consults on every request, so any write to it takes effect immediately and globally rather than requiring a second exploitation step. Attack path: Step 1 — attacker probes front door endpoints that accept a tenant/subscription identifier and issues a payload containing an appended statement targeting the tenant_role_bindings table (circumvents: parameterized-query expectation, since the value is string-concatenated). Step 2 — the injected write executes under the cloudapi service account, which was provisioned with INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE on role, policy, and binding tables for operational convenience (circumvents: intended read-mostly runtime role; no separate migration credential). Step 3 — the attacker widens their tenant's binding to a privileged role and deletes the policy row that scoped that role, so the per-request permission check on the front door now resolves to allow. Step 4 — the front door returns another tenant's vehicle records and permits remote commands outside the approved role scope, while deleted policy rows cause deny outcomes for legitimate calls, and the mutated tables destroy the audit baseline for what was actually authorized. The gap is the combination of string-built SQL in the front door's read path and a database role that can write the authorization tables — either one alone is survivable; together the authorization store becomes attacker-writable. Integrity is the directly violated property, so this maps to Tampering / A03 rather than to the confidentiality or repudiation effects that follow.

threat_statement: An attacker could alter data, configuration, or processing performed by Aurora directordb database after integrity validation or change controls are bypassed, resulting in the damage described by DS_10: The directordb is the record of truth the update-instruction signing service consults to determine which software version each vehicle's ECUs are currently running and which vehicles a given OTA campaign is permitted to target. If its integrity is compromised, signing decisions are made against false version or targeting data, so a vehicle can be recorded as already current and never receive a required software fix, or be signed for a campaign it does not belong to, leaving vehicles running incorrect or unapproved software with no reliable record of what is actually installed on them.
derivation_note: integrity maps to tampering under the STRIDE taxonomy. This deterministic fallback was used because the model did not return the required submit_threat tool call after two attempts.

threat_statement: Aurora pandoradb database: An attacker who can reach a provisioning or enrollment API that writes to the Aurora pandoradb vehicle_identity_enrollment and device_certificate_binding tables submits a crafted VIN and certificate-serial value that is concatenated into the provisioning statement instead of being bound as a parameter, and then issues a follow-up update that re-points an existing certificate_binding row at a different vehicle identity and inserts an extra enrollment row for a certificate the attacker controls; because pandoradb keeps the authoritative vehicle-to-certificate binding as ordinary mutable rows with no row-level signature and no append-only integrity check on those tables, the injected and rewritten rows are indistinguishable from records written by the legitimate provisioning flow; the platform reads that binding on every issuance and trust decision, so it issues and honours credentials for a device certificate that was never enrolled, accepting an unauthorized device as legitimately provisioned for a vehicle identity.
derivation_note: Selected tampering because the damage scenario's exploited property is integrity of the record set: the loss is not that the attacker reveals data (information disclosure) or is denied service, but that the authoritative vehicle-identity-to-certificate-binding content is silently rewritten so subsequent provisioning and certificate-validation decisions are made against forged data. The asset-specific mechanism is the write path into pandoradb's enrollment and certificate-binding tables combined with the absence of any integrity attestation (no per-row signature, no append-only/WORM guard, no independent reconciliation of binding rows against the CA's issuance log) — a generic "database compromise" statement would not name these tables, this binding semantic, or the fact that the platform re-reads the same rows as its trust decision, so the statement was derived around that mechanism rather than reusing a boilerplate database threat. The accompanying Spoofing and Elevation-of-Privilege consequences (a certificate accepted for the wrong vehicle identity, unauthorized device treated as enrolled) are the downstream effects of the same write and are not submitted separately here to avoid duplicating a single damage scenario.
